event.title: Andrew Barton, Ali Francis, and Lola Milholland in conversation
event.description: Literary Arts is excited to welcome author and journalist Ali Francis to celebrate her debut book, The Curious Lives of Vegetables, a wild journey through the hidden histories of plants. Francis will be joined by Portland writers Lola Milholland (Group Living and Other Recipes) and Andrew Barton (Free Food: earth eating, The Long Loaf, The Myrtlewood Cookbook) for a conversation moderated by environmental journalist and author Devon Fredericksen (How to Camp in the Woods). Together, they’ll explore what food can tell us about how we live: our relationships with plants and place, the ways knowledge and traditions move between people, what gets lost when food systems become less diverse, and what we might recover by paying closer attention to the things we eat. Moving from vegetables and biodiversity to bread, communal tables, regional foodways, and the everyday work of feeding people, the conversation will consider food not simply as something we consume, but as a reflection of our relationships with the natural world. About the book: Why are some carrots purple? What does a 1,000-year-old lotus seed have to tell us about survival? How did a tomato named for Paul Robeson become a political symbol? And what disappears when a vegetable disappears? In The Curious Lives of Vegetables, Australian journalist Ali Francis goes digging into the astonishing stories hiding in our crisper drawers, gardens, markets, and seed banks. Across more than 100 beautifully illustrated stories, she traces the plants we eat through migration and colonialism, politics and religion, extinction and revival, revealing vegetables as living records of human history — and essential seeds for a more resilient future. Along the way, Francis encounters ancient seeds brought back from the dead, vegetables carried across borders by displaced communities, plants transformed by centuries of human preference, and varieties now teetering on the edge of extinction. At once playful, deeply researched, and urgent, The Curious Lives of Vegetables asks us to look again at the ordinary plants on our plates, and to consider their extraordinary importance.

event.title: Writing Spirals: Multicultural Contemplations on Beginnings, Endings, and Cycles
event.description: The spiral holds great meaning for cultures all over the world and has captivated our attention throughout ancient and modern time. Whether of metaphysical and philosophical significance, or the many scientific and biological iterations of this powerful symbol, the multi-faceted spiral will be our muse. In this 3-part generative writing workshop, we’ll expand our writing across multiple genres including poetry, essay, and narrative with prompts inspired by multicultural authors. Thematically, we’ll move through Irish-Celtic mysticism, spiraling seasons of emergence, Afro-futurist science fiction, and our personal place within the great spiral. We’ll engage impactful elements of style and craft from our mentor texts like punctuation, dialogue, and symbol to enhance writing of resonance. Some time will be devoted to giving and receiving feedback as well as sharing in a supportive space. Writers of all levels and backgrounds are welcome. Course Outcomes Writers will: Explore a variety of multicultural texts as inspiration for writing. Draft poems, creative non-fiction, and narrative pieces related to spirals. Engage elements of craft and style from multigenre model texts. Enhance writing through feedback and sharing in positive and supportive circles. event.title: Kelly Grace Thomas in conversation with Joy Sullivan
event.description: The Literary Arts Bookstore & Cafe is excited to welcome author Kelly Grace Thomas to celebrate the release of her memoir-in-verse, Future Tense. Thomas will be joined in conversation by local poet Joy Sullivan. About the book: Reckoning with infertility, adoption, and love under pressure, Kelly Grace Thomas’s Future Tense is a searing memoir-in-verse about a woman’s fight to become a mother while losing her own. Thomas spends three years trying for a child who never arrives. As she struggles with infertility, her mother is dying of Stage IV uterine cancer, and the desire for a child turns urgent—a countdown. As her mother’s health deteriorates, time narrows, pressure builds, and the clock refuses to slow. As her marriage strains and the world remakes itself without her, Thomas refuses to give up. The fertility clinic is the coldest place on earth; still, she keeps going—through years of medical gaslighting, IVF consults, mounting debt, and backhanded blame—finally welcoming her daughter through adoption just months before her mother’s death. Intimate and unflinching, Future Tense interrogates the intertwined joys and griefs of womanhood and motherhood—and how biology can sometimes turn against us. Thomas approaches illness and loss with clarity and care, writing with a generosity that welcomes readers in. Despite their brevity, these poems refuse despair, finding meaning and connection even in the hardest seasons of life.

event.title: Nathaniel Hawthorne: Twice-Told Tales
event.description: When Henry James came to write his short classic book on his predecessor Nathaniel Hawthorne (who was an important influence on James), he wrote, with tongue in cheek, a description of the cultural and social wasteland that an ambitious American writer faced in Hawthorne’s day in finding material for fiction: No sovereign, no court,…no aristocracy, no church,…no army, no diplomatic service, no country gentlemen, no palaces, no castles, nor manors, nor old country-houses, nor parsonages, nor thatched cottages nor ivied ruins; no cathedrals, nor abbeys, nor little Norman churches; no great Universities nor public schools; no literature, no novels, no museums, no pictures, no political society, no sporting class…. Some such list as that might be drawn up of the absent things in American life, the effect of which,…upon an English or a French imagination, would probably as a general thing be appalling. And yet Hawthorne, as James well knew, in his most memorable works created a brilliant array of imaginative fictions drawn from the riches of New England life—its legends, tall tales, landscapes, and history. Rather than being appalled, Hawthorne, as James well knew, in his most memorable works created a brilliant array of imaginative fictions drawn from the riches of New England life—its legends, tall tales, landscapes, and history This Delve seminar will focus on Hawthorne’s short stories—among the most thrilling, strange, and memorable in the American canon. We will explore his first collection of stories, Twice-Told Tales (1837, 1851) as well as a small selection of extraordinary later stories. Hawthorne worked his American materials in a diverse range of genres—horror, the gothic, romance, the fantastic, moral tales, allegory—and narrative subjects—ambiguities of love and loss, gender and sex, guilt, conflicts between authority and non-conformists, secrets, science and magic, modernity and tradition, past and present, shadows, and a repudiation of tyranny. What marks all the works we will delve into during this seminar is mystery, ambiguity, thrills and chills, and a keen sense of the ways in which power seeks to dominate the individual. These characteristics alone make him our contemporary. Writer and Hawthorne fan Rosemary Mahoney writes: Whatever form they take, Twice-Told Tales, like salt and sugar on daily staples, are a kind of splendid seasoning, coaxing into acuteness the full, strange flavor of life…. Sit this evening by your brownest lamp and read these stories. If you find yourself unstirred, unengaged, un-creeped, then perhaps—and I propose this in the politest way possible—you should check your pulse. Texts: We will use the Modern Library Classics edition of Twice-Told Tales, with an introduction by Mahoney, plus a few stories from his other collections of short stories to be supplied in pdf. event.title: Nature Writing
event.description: Throughout this six week course, students will look at the many ways in which humans are connected to our natural surroundings, both urban and remote. Weather, soil, plants, wildlife, changing systems, and more will all be explored. By delving into the inherent close relationship humans have with our natural world, each student’s path to writing their own stories using the natural world as scaffolding will emerge. Each lesson will be designed to unlock the storyteller within by encouraging observation, reading, and learning about natural systems. Participants will read various forms of nature prose and poetry including work by Mary Oliver, Robin Wall Kimmerer, Barbara Kingsolver, Merlin Sheldrake, Richard Powers, Robert Macfarlane, and more. These readings and the resulting discussions will then serve as a springboard to developing personal tone and style. Through guided in-class exercises students will work to develop their own narrative voice. Each step in the course will hone in on students’ unique narrative perspectives that reflects their own personal connections to the natural world. The in-class writing prompts will often draw on lived experiences and are intended to help students find their voice. Whether it’s remembering a favorite hike, gardening in their own backyard, watching a bird from their apartment window, cloud watching, traveling further afield into the wilderness, swimming, or walking a creek path, students will have opportunities to use memory to capture the feeling of decompressing in nature in words. Students will explore various forms and literary devices and styles in the process. Students will then have the opportunity to share these free-writes in class to get feedback from peers and the instructor. By reading the greats and engaging with the natural world from a personal standpoint, students will develop their understanding of ecology and our human connection to it as a species. By the end of the course, acknowledging human interconnectivity with nature may very well become an inherent part of students’ writing process. This course invites students to dig deep, observe the world around them, slow down, bask in the beauty of the PNW, and discover how their own unique stories can spring from nature. event.title: Michael Lewis in conversation with David Shipley
event.description: Literary Arts is pleased to present #1 New York Times bestselling author and host of Apple’s #1 rated podcast Against the Rules, Michael Lewis, in conversation with The New York Times editor-at-large David Shipley, about his new book, Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State. If you’re a high school educator interested in bringing students to this event, please contact our Director of Youth Programs at olivia@literary-arts.org About the book: In Blockers, Lewis views the “meteor strike” of the second Trump administration through the eyes of the public servants targeted by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). As he says, “Every now and then the world hands you the material for a wild story. The collision between the Trump administration and the civil service is one of those moments. “I’ve had so much fun writing this book that at times it has been hard to know whether to laugh or cry.” As Lewis explains, in the new Washington, being a Blocker was the worst thing you could be—especially if you worked in the federal government and wanted to keep your job. A Blocker was a holdover, an impediment, someone who didn’t get the message—and, most of all, someone who didn’t belong. In Blockers Lewis tells the story of seven people who believed they had a calling, who were convinced they were doing something the country couldn’t do without, and then discovered they were no longer wanted. One kept Americans’ most sensitive tax data out of the wrong hands, and another made sure that politicians and civil servants played by the rules. One figured out how to stop wildfires from destroying suburban neighborhoods, another helped uncover the mysteries of cystic fibrosis. There was also a security guard. It should come as no surprise that the writer who made subprime mortgages gripping (The Big Short) and turned baseball statistics into poetry (Moneyball) could transform the first two years of the second Trump administration into a thriller about federal employees. But he does. And he also puts before us a clear question: If these public servants can’t survive in government today, then what does that say about us? event.description: The Literary Arts Bookstore and Cafe are thrilled to welcome Lit Mic for another immersive writing workshop! Participants will search for clues, interview witnesses, and conduct their own investigation via creative writing prompts and sharing to solve the murder. Detective Jack Argentine is back, and this time, it’s magical. It’s nearly Halloween, and a coven of honest-to-goodness witches is hosting their Biannual Bewitchment Ball. But something has gone terribly wrong, and one of the coven members is dead! Through independent and guided writing prompts, investigation, and conversations with live witchy actors, it’s up to YOU to help Detective Argentine figure out if this is just a spell gone wrong… or a case of Halloween Homicide. But the witching hour is close at hand; if the clock strikes midnight, the witches will be gone back to their home, and this case will vanish like mist in the night. Are you up for the task? About Lit Mic: Portland Lit Mic is a community-oriented organization, dedicated to getting writers from all backgrounds together. Founded as a writers-only open mic by Portland State Alumni Jordan Marzka and Grace Lawrence, the two have gone on to plan and host immersive writing workshops and reading series. event.title: Journalism for Every Writer
event.description: Journalism isn’t only for journalists. The practice involves skills that are useful to any and all writers across genres and levels of experience. At its core, reporting is the process of asking questions and seeking answers, which is something all writers do in one form or another. In addition to interviews, research is a valuable tool for any writer to deepen and expand their understanding of a chosen subject and fact-checking can heighten the rigor and truth of any work, even the most fantastical fiction. As part of their training, journalists learn how to distill a story down to its core components, make it legible to a wide audience, and structure information to maximize impact. These are skills and practices that all writers can benefit from. Whether there’s a journalist character in your novel, a historical component to your memoir, a narrative aspect to your academic work, or a poem that provides a glimpse into an unknown world, this class will provide a basic understanding of journalism that any writer can apply to any project. Course outcomes: ● Writers are introduced to the fundamentals of reporting, research, writing, editing and fact-checking ● Writers explore how to incorporate these skills into their writing practice ● Writers gain confidence applying these skills in their own projects, outside of the classroom Class schedule: Week 1: The Journalist Mindset—Week 1 provides an overarching introduction to the key concepts of journalism and how it can be applied to any writing project. Concepts include the “5 Ws + H” and newsworthiness. Week 2: Reporting and Research—Students will learn interview techniques; discuss other ways to access information, like court documents, public records and archives; and review best practices for research, like relying on primary source documents and vetting journal articles. Week 3: Writing & Structure—How to write and structure a basic news story, with a discussion of how those core principles (like the inverted pyramid) can apply to any writing project. It will also address how to approach writing a feature story, which requires using information to build scenes and character development. Week 4: Ethics & Accuracy—How to fact-check and why it matters. Students will learn what goes into fact-checking and how to ensure that the information they have gathered is accurate. They will also learn core ethical principles of journalism, such as objectivity, independence, as well as how to handle attribution (on vs off the record) and how to handle sources requesting anonymity or who are not telling the truth. Week 5: Organization and Pitching. In this session, students will get tips on how to keep all their reporting notes and material organized to help streamline the writing, editing and fact-checking process. The class will also cover the basics and best practices of pitching so students feel empowered to send their ideas out into the world. Week 6: Workshop. The final class will be dedicated to discussing each student’s ideas and providing collective guidance and feedback. Whether it’s a question about a story’s angle or a full-fledged pitch, this session will be a forum for everyone to take their journalistic aspirations to the next level, incorporating what they’ve learned over the past five weeks. event.title: Theodor Adorno: Minima Moralia
event.description: When the nation and culture you grew up in and love have been taken over by a war-waging fascist dictatorship, how do you come to understand the nature and causes of what has happened? Perhaps you can do this only after you fled for your life. How then would you look at the ruins left inside yourself? This was the situation faced by one of the most sophisticated and profound thinkers of the twentieth century, Theodor Adorno (1903–1969), when he found himself living in Los Angeles during World War II after escaping from Nazi Germany. In this Delve we will study Adorno’s Minima Moralia: Reflections from Damaged Life—the amazing book he wrote between 1944 and 1949 to explore his feelings about the calamitous situation of a world facing despotism. We will read the entire book and focus on selected essays. The book is made up of 153 very short essays, ranging from 1-3 pages. The essays focus his philosophical genius on deeply observed and subtle aspects of ourselves that contribute to or resist the ways in which we are socialized that result in alienation, loss of will and agency, and unfulfillment. He explores consumer culture, the arts, and politics along with his recollections of the rise of fascism. Each essay is a deep and intricate knot of feelings and ideas, presented by a contemplative, perseverant, unblinking thinker of the highest order Although written in grief, Adorno always seeks hope by confronting, with maximum honesty and penetration, the deep roots of the problems human society faces. Minima Moralia is a monument to the sensitive study of culture and our psyches amidst disaster trauma. Adorno’s brilliant and strong style make this book a pleasure to think with. In this Delve we will read the entire book and focus on selected entries. Text: Minima Moralia: Reflections from Damaged Life<, Theodor Adorno, translator E. F. N. event.title: Claire Keegan: Small Things Like These  and Foster
event.description: In rating Small Things Like These 41st on its list of the 100 Best Books of the 21st Century, the New York Times said: “Not a word is wasted in Keegan’s small, burnished gem of a novel, a sort of Dickensian miniature….” This is an important novella in the vein of Dickens’s A Christmas Carol, but with an ending that packs a different punch. At its center is a man torn between family, community, church, and one young woman in a terrible predicament. He must make a choice, and Keegan’s exquisite, concise writing reveals that agonizing choice. It’s a perfect story to ponder and discuss: What would you choose in his situation? Keegan’s other work, “Foster,” is a long short story with a big impact. No word is wasted as Keegan tells the story of a young girl sent to live with another family when her own mother is fraught with problems of her own. Again, in the New York Times’s glowing review they say: “Keegan makes us complicit in what her characters want, setting us up for utter heartbreak when they don’t get it.” Foster’s is already considered canonical and is taught as a required text for Comparative Literature in the curriculum for Ireland’s secondary schools. Join us in this two-week exploration of these incredible short works by an Irish writer of spare prose and mmense talent. event.title: Rebecca Handler in conversation with Selina Fillinger
event.description: The Literary Arts Bookstore is pleased to welcome author Rebecca Handler to celebrate her new novel, In the Round. Handler will be joined in conversation by Selina Fillinger. About the book: Have you ever been dead certain that you’re being observed, that maybe your very existence is predicated on how others see you? A few minutes after she’s become convinced she’s the victim of a home invasion, In the Round’s brilliant and intimate narrator plunges us into a feminist Kafkaesque literary mystery that unfolds over the course of one weird—and dare we say, dramatic—night in San Francisco. Nothing is missing from her family’s home, but everything feels wrong. So begins a sleepless night of questioning, and a novel packed with the kind of astonishing twists that leave readers wondering: Is all the world a stage, after all? Over the course of the evening, theatrical elements creep in: a cast list, a prop list, an intermission. At once an avant-garde thriller, a meditation on motherhood and mortality, a full-throated endorsement of gut-level intuition, and a tribute to the rapture of live theater in a post-pandemic world, In the Round is a lively, inventive, and completely singular story.

event.title: The Moth Mainstage: Tightrope
event.description: This December, The Moth’s anticipated Mainstage season comes to Portland in partnership with Literary Arts. One foot in front of another… Join The Moth this fall for TIGHTROPE, an evening of extraordinary true stories about what happens when there’s no clear path—only the courage to keep moving forward. Stories of balancing without a net. Trusting your gut. Taking the leap before you know where you’ll land. Of big gambles and near misses, quiet acts of bravery and glorious mistakes. Of sending the text, booking the flight, sharing the secret you’ve carried for years, and watching everything change. The Mainstage tour is The Moth’s signature live show, featuring a carefully curated lineup of tellers—writers, artists, adventurers, community members, and unexpected voices—sharing true personal stories, told live and without notes. Come spend an evening on the edge. One step can change the whole story. About The Moth The Moth is a global storytelling nonprofit with the mission to inspire people to listen and share openly, think and feel deeply, and expand their understanding of one another. Since 1997, The Moth has presented more than 70,000 true stories—told live and without notes—in 11 countries, across 4 continents. Today, The Moth produces 600+ live shows annually, as well as the Peabody Award-winning The Moth Radio Hour, and the popular The Moth Podcast. Through workshops for students, educators, adults, advocates, and professionals, The Moth guides thousands of new storytellers each year in finding and sharing their own voices. event.title: Charles Dickens: Our Mutual Friend
event.description: Some critics of British 19th century novels place Dickens’s final completed novel, Our Mutual Friend, alongside other great novels of that era: Middlemarch, by George Eliot; Vanity Fair, by William Makepeace Thackeray; The Way We Live Now, by Anthony Trollope; and Jane Eyre, by Charlotte Bronte. This novel is darker, more brooding, than any of those. Rather than years or decades in his past to create a feeling of nostalgia, at the end of his 40th year as a published writer and most of the time the most famous and popular writer in the English language, Dickens turns his pen onto a satiric look London’s pursuit of Money and Society, and a bitter one at the state of the poor and those whose living are derived from the great and polluted River Thames, the powerful controlling symbol that unites many of the characters and plots in the novel. In this six-week Delve we will discuss those issues, the novel’s place in Dickens’s development as an artist, and experience a novel filled with death, deceit, riverside dives, and disguises. event.title: From Changemaker to Author: A Nonfiction Book Development Intensive
event.description: If you’re looking to become known for an idea and respected for your expertise – it’s time to write your nonfiction book. You already have something to say. You’ve said it in rooms, in conversations, in work that has changed people. But the book? That feels like a different thing entirely – bigger, more elusive, somehow always not quite the right time. This six-week intensive is for the writer who has lived their subject matter. The expert, the advocate, the practitioner, the person who has earned their perspective and is ready to shape it into something that lasts. Each session combines direct instruction with hands-on writing practice, guided research, breakout group work, and mastermind-style coaching — so students leave every class with something made, not just something learned. A craft thread runs through every session: every workshop produces actual writing, not just planning documents. Who this class is for: Nonfiction writers at any stage and any publishing path — whether you have a full draft, a half-formed concept, or simply the deep certainty that there is a book inside you. No prior publishing experience required. Especially well-suited to practitioners, educators, advocates, and entrepreneurs who want to translate their expertise into a book. Class Schedule: Week 1: Why this book, why you, why now. Types of nonfiction and publishing paths overview. The identity question: who gets to write a book, and why that question is worth examining before you write a word. Workshop: draft your three whys and write the first version of your “why you” paragraph — the one that answers why you are the only person who can write this book. Week 2: Prove there’s a reader. Market analysis, comp analysis, finding the gap your book fills. How to read a comp not just as a sales tool but as a craft model. Workshop: guided research session, comp identification, group share-out. Each student writes one paragraph of market analysis for their own book. Week 3: Build the architecture. Book structure — chronological, topical, problem-solution. The difference between a book idea and a book argument. Finding your hook. Workshop: draft a chapter framework and write your opening hook — the first sentence or paragraph that earns the reader’s attention. Breakout groups workshop each other’s hooks and structures. Optional guest author perspective on structure. Week 4: Your voice on the page. What makes nonfiction writing compelling rather than merely informational. Voice, specificity, the role of personal story even in prescriptive work. How to write toward your reader without losing yourself. Workshop: generative writing exercise — each student writes a scene, anecdote, or opening that demonstrates their voice. Mastermind-style coaching on what’s working and where to push further. Week 5: Your author identity and platform. Who you are before the book comes out matters as much as who you are after. Platform audit — what you already have, what you need, how to build now. PR angles, community strategy, the difference between an audience and a platform. Publishing paths in depth and how early decisions shape later options. Workshop: draft your author bio. Mastermind-style coaching on individual platform gaps and publishing path decisions. Week 6: Showcase and next steps. Each student presents their concept to the group: their why, their reader, their structure, their hook, their voice. Structured peer feedback. Optional guest — a working author, publisher, or agent. Every student leaves with a written concept overview, a comp list, a structural framework, a voice sample, and an author bio draft. Students pursuing traditional publishing leave with the bones of a proposal. Students going indie leave with a positioning and launch strategy. Goals and Outcomes: A clearly defined book concept with working title and core argument A comp list and market analysis paragraph A chapter-by-chapter structural framework A written opening hook and voice sample A drafted author bio A clear publishing path and next steps, whether traditional, hybrid, or independent A peer community of nonfiction writers to carry the work forward Access Program We want our writing classes and seminars to be accessible to everyone, regardless of income and background. event.title: After: Poems in Conversation
event.description: No poem is written alone. Every poem is in conversation with the writing that came before it. This conversation crosses generations and cultures, erasing distances of time, space, and mortality. In this four-part class, we’ll make that conversation intentional. We’ll consider the what, why, and how of writing in dialogue with other writers: what it means to write “after” someone, why we might quote, echo, erase, or respond to another text, and how we might do so with care, integrity, and proper credit. We’ll read poems by historical and contemporary poets who write in conversation with other poets, novelists, essayists, scientists, journalists, and historical documents. Approaches we’ll consider include: the epigraph and homage, collage and quotation, the cento, found poetry, erasure, and the response poem. In our first two classes, we’ll read examples and try generative exercises. In our second two classes, we’ll share our work and offer supportive feedback on each other’s conversations. No previous experience in writing poetry is required; all are welcome. Access Program We want our writing classes and seminars to be accessible to everyone, regardless of income and background. event.title: Reading & Looking
event.description: Join us for a Delve seminar in which we will explore a wide range of visual art alongside short essays and books by artists, novelists, philosophers, filmmakers, and poets. Together we will read a series of classic unconventional short texts, both old and new, that examine the complex roles color (culminating with a deep dive into the color blue) plays in literature, the fine arts, philosophy, music, and daily life. We are said to be a visual culture, but few people read images as critically as text. To sharpen our seeing in both forms is what this seminar hopes to achieve, as critical reading in one deepens the experience of the other. Together we will consider such questions as: how do we “read” an image as opposed to a text and vice versa? What are the similarities and differences between verbal and visual media? Our gateway into the world of color will be two classic essays by art critic and Booker Prize winning novelist John Berger devoted to some of the earliest artistic visions extant: the Paleolithic drawings found in Chauvet cave and the mesmerizing Fayum portraits from Greco-Roman Egypt. We will follow these pieces with two sessions on Derek Jarman’s book Chroma: A Book of Color—a genre-bending memoir that examines the color spectrum and its effect on memory in a series of insightful, playful short chapters, written as he was losing his sight at the end of his life. Eventually Jarman was able to see only in shades of blue—circumstances that make his ruminations on color both powerful and poignant. Our next session will take us into Ludwig Wittgenstein’s mind-expanding thoughts on color perception via excerpts from his Remarks on Color, which we couple with painter and writer Amy Sillman’s insights into how artists approach color—both explore their struggle with words to convey the rich spectrum of experience. The seminar culminates with two sessions on Maggie Nelson’s Bluets, an equally genre-bending experiment in autobiography—an exploration of how we see (or what we miss) and a love letter to blue as color, mood (loss, joy), and its role in art and in life. Alongside these readings, in each session, using the large screen in Literary Arts’ seminar room, we will look at works of art (both painting and photography ranging from the very oldest work to contemporary art) that are either referred to in the texts or that can be placed in fruitful conversation with the readings. Together we will take a chromophilic journey into the realms of vision, visual pleasure, language, and literature. Texts: Chroma: A Book of Color by Derak Jarman Bluets by Maggie Nelson Excerpts from Wittgenstein and the essays by Berger and Sillman will be supplied by PDF. Participants will be sent files of the images we will be discussing prior to each session. event.title: Everybody Reads 2027: Louise Erdrich
event.description: Literary Arts is pleased to present New York Times bestselling author Louise Erdrich at the Arlene Schnitzer Concert Hall on March 18, 2027. Her appearance will conclude months of engaging programs and events through Multnomah County Library’s Everybody Reads program, a community-wide project that promotes shared reading and discussion around a single book. Erdrich’s 2025 novel, The Mighty Red, is the library’s 2027 reading selection and the focal point of this year’s Everybody Reads. From January through March, library-led discussions and activities will center on the book’s themes around love, family, time, and the complexities of being human. About the book: In this stunning novel, Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award–winning author Louise Erdrich tells a story of love, natural forces, spiritual yearnings, and the tragic impact of uncontrollable circumstances on ordinary people’s lives. In the Red River Valley of North Dakota, several lives revolve around a wedding fraught with desire, jealousy, and uncertainty. Gary Geist, a terrified young man set to inherit two farms, is desperate to marry Kismet Poe, an impulsive, lapsed goth who can’t read her own future but will settle for fulfilling his. Her best friend, Hugo, a gentle, red-haired, homeschooled giant, also loves Kismet and is determined to steal her away and build a life together. Kismet’s mother, Crystal, drives a truck for Gary’s family, and on her nightly runs, tunes in to the darkness of late-night radio, experiences visions of guardian angels, and worries about what’s to come, for her daughter and herself. The Mighty Red is Louise Erdrich at her consummate best. A novel of tender humor, disquietude, yearning, community, and family, it is about ordinary people who dream, grow up, fall in love, struggle, endure tragedy, carry bitter secrets; men and women both complicated and contradictory, flawed and decent, lonely and hopeful. Human time, deep time, Red River time, and geological time are explored alongside the impact of crises in our own time—climate change, the depletion of natural resources, the economic meltdown of 2008. It is a story about our tattered bond with the earth, and about love in all of its absurdity and splendor.
